links.outcome: Omissions in ambient AI scribe notes (symptom duration, important details)
links.effect: Symptom duration appeared in the chief complaint of 17% (8/47) of AI notes; 55.3% (26/47) of students agreed the AI note left out important details.
links.quote: Post hoc analysis of AI notes revealed that symptom duration, an explicit criterion required for full QNOTE credit in the chief complaint element, was mentioned in the chief complaint section in 17% (8/47) of the AI notes.

links.outcome: Note quality change after incorporating AI note (overreliance on flawed output)
links.effect: Chief complaint scores declined (P=.05), with fully acceptable 34% vs 44.7% and unacceptable 14.9% vs 6.4%; other 9 elements similar; 10.6% (5/47) declined ≥20 points.
links.quote: In paired analysis of QNOTE elements between human-only and hybrid notes among AI scribe participants, the largest element-level change was a decline in chief complaint scores ( P =.05) driven by fewer “fully acceptable” (16/47, 34% vs 21/47, 44.7%) and more “unacceptable” (7/47, 14.9% vs 3/47, 6.4%) hybrid notes as compared to human-only notes, respectively.

links.outcome: Omission of symptom duration from AI-generated chief complaint sections
links.effect: Symptom duration, required for full QNOTE credit, appeared in the chief complaint section in only 17% (8/47) of AI notes.
links.quote: Post hoc analysis of AI notes revealed that symptom duration, an explicit criterion required for full QNOTE credit in the chief complaint element, was mentioned in the chief complaint section in 17% (8/47) of the AI notes.

links.outcome: Deterioration in chief complaint documentation after students reviewed AI notes
links.effect: Chief complaint scores declined (P=.05). Hybrid versus human-only notes were less often fully acceptable (16/47, 34% vs 21/47, 44.7%) and more often unacceptable (7/47, 14.9% vs 3/47, 6.4%).
links.quote: In paired analysis of QNOTE elements between human-only and hybrid notes among AI scribe participants, the largest element-level change was a decline in chief complaint scores ( P =.05) driven by fewer “fully acceptable” (16/47, 34% vs 21/47, 44.7%) and more “unacceptable” (7/47, 14.9% vs 3/47, 6.4%) hybrid notes as compared to human-only notes, respectively.

links.effect: Symptom duration was mentioned in the chief complaint section in only 17% (8/47) of the AI notes.
links.quote: Symptom duration, an explicit criterion required for full QNOTE credit in the chief complaint element, was mentioned in the chief complaint section in 17% (8/47) of the AI notes.

links.effect: Chief complaint scores declined because AI notes often omitted symptom duration, a locally required criterion for full credit.
links.quote: The difference in chief complaint scores was likely due to conciseness in AI notes that often omitted symptom duration, an explicit criterion for full credit on QNOTE.

links.outcome: incorporation of omissions into final note
links.effect: In paired analysis, hybrid notes had significantly lower chief complaint scores (P=.05) with fewer fully acceptable notes than human-only notes due to automation bias.
links.quote: In paired analysis of QNOTE elements between human-only and hybrid notes among AI scribe participants, the largest element-level change was a decline in chief complaint scores ( P =.05) driven by fewer “fully acceptable” (16/47, 34% vs 21/47, 44.7%) and more “unacceptable” (7/47, 14.9% vs 3/47, 6.4%) hybrid notes as compared to human-only notes, respectively.

links.effect: 21.3% of students agreed that regular use of the AI scribe could reduce their ability to learn how to write a good note.
links.quote: In total, 21.3% (10/47) agreed or strongly agreed that the AI write-up “when used regularly, may reduce my ability to learn how to write a good note” ( Figure 3 ).
